CBET Exam Cost, Dates, and Retake Rules in 2026

The CBET is not an exam you can book on a Tuesday for the following Monday. It runs on windows, the application closes well before the window opens, and the fee is the smallest part of the budget. Here is the whole picture for 2026 so you can put real dates on a plan.

The fee

The 2026 exam fee is $410 for AAMI members and $460 for non-members. Membership is optional and you can sit the exam without it. The $50 difference does not by itself justify joining, so decide on membership for its own reasons and treat the exam fee as a flat cost either way.

The windows and the lead time

The exam is offered twice a year, in May and November, at computer-based test centers. Applications usually open about three months before a window, which is the number that actually governs your calendar. Work backwards from it.

Target window      Watch for applications      Start studying
May                around February             the previous autumn
November           around August               the previous spring

Six months of steady study is a reasonable plan for someone already working as a technician. Three months is possible if your day job covers most of the content and you have a focused review system. One month is a gamble on 165 questions.

Candidate status versus full certification

This decides whether you can apply at all, so check it before you budget anything.

Full certification requires one of three combinations:

  • An associate degree or higher in electronics, technology, or science, plus two years of full-time BMET work.
  • A United States military biomedical equipment technology program, plus two years of full-time BMET work.
  • Four years of full-time BMET work with no degree.

Candidate status requires only one piece of that: the degree alone, the military program alone, or two years of full-time work alone. A candidate who passes the exam has five years to complete the remaining requirements and upgrade to full certification. For a recent graduate this is the better deal. You sit the exam while the coursework is still sharp, and the certificate converts as your hours accumulate.

What the exam day looks like

165 questions in 3 hours, closed book, with an on-screen calculator. That is about 65 seconds per question, which is why timed practice matters more than re-reading notes. Passing is around 116 correct, roughly 70 percent, with the cut score set by the issuing body using a criterion-referenced method rather than a fixed pass rate.

Retakes

A failed attempt means a new application for a later window, so a November miss points at the following May. Build that into your thinking before you sit: a borderline attempt taken too early does not just cost the fee, it costs six months. The practical rule is to only apply once your own practice scores are comfortably above 70 percent, not at it.

What to budget beyond the fee

  • Travel and time off. Test centers are not everywhere. Price the drive, and if the nearest center is far enough to need a hotel, add it now rather than in April.
  • AAMI membership, if you want it, at whatever the current rate is. Optional, as above.
  • Study material. Standards references and equipment theory texts are the traditional route and they are not cheap. A structured course plus a good practice bank covers most candidates for less.
  • Recertification. Every three years, with continuing education. The cost is mostly your time, but conference or training fees land in the same bucket, so it belongs in a career budget rather than a surprise.
  • A small bench. A multimeter and a handful of components are cheap and they make the electronics domain concrete instead of abstract.

A simple plan for a November sitting

  1. Spring: read through the full body of knowledge once and mark what you have never touched at work.
  2. Early summer: work the weak domains with practice questions, not rereading. Safety, standards, and electronics repay drilling the most.
  3. August: watch for applications to open and submit yours. Confirm which status you are applying under.
  4. September and October: full-length timed sets at the real pace, 165 questions in 3 hours, until three of your last five attempts clear 80 percent.
  5. The last week: no new material. Review your own wrong answers and the numbers you have to know cold.
The one scheduling mistake to avoid is studying hard all spring and discovering in September that applications closed in August. Put the application date in your calendar before you put the study plan in it.

Questions people ask

How much does the CBET cost in 2026?

The 2026 exam fee is $410 for AAMI members and $460 for non-members. Membership is optional, and the $50 gap is small enough that it only pays for itself if you also want the other member benefits.

When can I take the CBET?

There are two windows a year, one in May and one in November, at computer-based test centers. Applications generally open about three months before a window, so the realistic planning milestones are February and August.

What is the difference between candidate and full status?

Full certification needs a degree plus two years of BMET work, the military biomedical program plus two years, or four years of work alone. Candidate status needs only one of those pieces, and a candidate who passes has five years to finish the rest and upgrade.

What score do I need to pass?

Roughly 116 correct out of 165, about 70 percent. The issuing body sets the cut score with a criterion-referenced method, so treat 70 percent as the planning target and build a margin above it.

How often do I have to recertify?

Every three years, with continuing education. Start logging your training hours the month you pass rather than scrambling in year three.
